title: Know the data
text: This case concerns recorded COVID-19 occurrence in 31 mainland Chinese provincial units during the 12 months of 2020 . The outcome is binary: 0 = no occurrence; 1 = occurrence . The source manual describes National Health Commission records, remote-sensing and environmental indicators, and Baidu mobility data. File / field Meaning Covid_Binary_Panel.xlsx Original wide table: 31 rows, with monthly columns; convert before modeling COVID-19-Ready-Panel.csv Added ready-to-import panel: 372 rows, preserved values China Provincial Map/China Provincial Map.* 31-unit map, with the shared gb identifier gb Province code; preserve exact values and check its imported type Month 1 through 12, representing January–December 2020 covid Binary response in the ready panel and recommended conversion PM25, Temp, NDVI, NTL Air quality, temperature, vegetation, and nighttime-light indicators Total_In, Total_Out Interprovincial incoming and outgoing mobility indices A filename is not a data-format guarantee. Despite its Panel filename, the original workbook is wide. Either follow the conversion below or import COVID-19-Ready-Panel.csv directly and continue at step 2. The latter skips conversion, but never skips Data Check. Inspect mobility missingness before fitting. Total_In and Total_Out each contain 93 missing entries out of 372 records (25%). The other four predictors and the binary response are complete. The ready panel preserves these missing values. Record how they are handled and consider a clearly labeled sensitivity analysis rather than silently treating missing mobility as zero.

title: 5. Interpret effects and relative contribution
text: The temporal and spatial coefficients are on the model’s log-odds scale. A positive coefficient indicates an association with higher modeled odds conditional on the specification; it is not an absolute increase in probability. Standardized predictors change the unit of coefficient interpretation. STVPI can summarize relative factor contributions and their uncertainty. In the documented desktop version, logistic models lack the residual component needed for the overall model explainable percentage. Do not label a relative contribution chart as total explained outcome variation. Source example: monthly temporal coefficients and credible intervals. Click to enlarge. Source example: spatial coefficient maps for the binary model. Click to enlarge. Source example: relative spatiotemporal contribution components. Click to enlarge.

title: 6. Examine probabilities and predictive discrimination
text: Read predict_y as a predicted probability and verify it lies between 0 and 1. Map probabilities using a common 0–1 scale across months. If a decision needs a yes/no label, state a justified threshold; do not assume a threshold was automatically validated by the model. An ROC curve plots sensitivity against the false-positive rate over thresholds. AUC summarizes discrimination, but does not assess calibration and is not a causal result. The source figure below is a historical fitted-data illustration. For a prediction claim, use held-out data, exclude records with unavailable outcomes, and report how validation was designed. Historical binary example: ROC curve and AUC, illustrating discrimination. Click to enlarge. Historical binary example: monthly predicted probability maps. Click to enlarge. The R accuracy example fixes the positive class to 1 and the ROC direction, so the evaluation follows the stated event definition rather than choosing the direction from the data.

title: 7. Save a reproducible record
text: Keep the original wide workbook, converted or ready panel, checked data, map components, settings, result workbook, and missingness notes together. Continue to Understand results and R visualization , or try the smaller count case .

title: Know the data
text: The source case combines global health, socioeconomic, environmental, and behavioral indicators for 2000–2020 . The supplied map contains 177 unique spatial identifiers ; the CSV contains 3,717 unique location–year records (177 × 21). Its spatial IDs match the map. Sources described in the manual include GBD, GIOVANNI, the World Bank, and air-quality data. File / field Meaning TestData_Continuous.csv Original panel table; no wide-to-long conversion required TestMap_Continuous.* Complete world map component set ISO_A3 Shared map and panel identifier; case sensitive Year 2000 through 2020 HALE Health-adjusted life expectancy, the response Y3, NE3, NE7, HB2, HB6, PM2.5 Six predictors in the introductory model The source dictionary identifies Y3 as maternal mortality, NE3 as NDVI, HB2 as high body-mass index, and HB6 as vitamin A deficiency. PM2.5 is an air-pollution indicator. Neither source manual defines NE7 , so this guide retains its field code without assigning a name or unit. Several source unit labels are inconsistent, so do not infer measurement units or transformations from those labels alone. Missing values are part of this case. The supplied CSV contains 273 missing HALE outcomes. Missing entries among the six selected predictors range from 273 to 582. Preserve NA values, inspect missingness, and record how the model handles them. A complete location–year grid is not the same as complete measurements.

title: 4. Read coefficients and contribution
text: Open model.evaluation first to inspect the completed model and diagnostic measures. Use time.coefficients to examine temporal variation, space.coefficients for geographic variation, and STVPI for model-based contribution with uncertainty. Display 95% and 50% credible intervals alongside means. A colored spatial coefficient map is a map of a modeled association; it is not a map of causal effects. Read the coefficient-scale guidance before comparing directions or magnitudes. Source example: temporal coefficients with 95% and 50% uncertainty bands. Click to enlarge. title: 5. Inspect prediction on the response scale
text: In local.prediction , y denotes the observed outcome, predict_y the response-scale prediction, and fill_y an outcome field with missing values filled. Continuous model output also contains log-scale summaries. The source workflow already back-transforms the columns with the predict_ prefix: do not exponentiate them again. Compare observed and predicted values only where both exist. RMSE summarizes error in the response units; R² is relative to a mean-only reference and can be negative. Agreement on the fitted training data is descriptive performance, not independent validation. Use a suitable held-out design for claims about forecasting. The manual uses a separate 12-predictor prediction example. For that optional extension, fit a new model with Y3, HB1, HB2, HB6, SE3, SE5, SE6, SE7, SE9, NE2, NE3, and PM2.5, and save HALE12_all_result.xlsx. The prediction figures below belong to this expanded example. Do not expect a six-predictor run to reproduce their numerical metrics. text: You should now have a checked panel, a saved settings record, and a workbook with the six result sections. title: Know the data
text: The source case combines acute hepatitis B surveillance counts with socioeconomic and environmental indicators in five Appalachian states: Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia . The study period is 2012–2023 . The source manual identifies CDC, ACS, and NOAA as data sources. title: 5. Read time, space, and contribution
text: Count-model coefficients describe associations on the log scale of the modeled mean. They are not directly changes in the number of cases. Keep credible intervals in view when discussing direction, magnitude, and variation. Standardization changes a predictor’s interpretation from one raw unit to a standardized unit. Plot temporal means with both 95% and 50% credible bands. If you add a LOESS curve for visual guidance, retain the original annual points; that smoother is a display layer rather than a new posterior estimate. For maps, join spatial coefficients using GEOID. As with the binary case, the documented Poisson desktop model does not supply the residual component needed for an overall model explainable percentage. Interpret STVPI as the available relative factor contribution, within the model’s scope. Source example: count-model temporal coefficients and uncertainty. Click to enlarge. Source example: smoothed temporal display with the original annual estimates. Click to enlarge. Source example: spatial coefficient maps for PD, POV, PRECIP, and UNINS. Click to enlarge. Source example: relative spatiotemporal contribution and uncertainty. Click to enlarge.

title: 6. Assess count predictions
text: Inspect local.prediction and confirm that predict_y is a predicted mean on the count scale. A mean prediction can be fractional; it is not a newly observed integer case count. If an export contains only a linear predictor, confirm the appropriate transformation before using count metrics. Compare predictions with observed COUNT values. Mean absolute error (MAE) describes the average absolute error in case counts. Mean Poisson deviance respects the count response scale; define the zero-count contribution correctly. A deviance-based pseudo-R² compares that deviance to a mean-only reference and can be negative. Validation and missing-value handling have different purposes. There are no missing outcomes in this supplied case. The source code’s NA filtering is a general example, not evidence of missing observations here. Historical fitted-data accuracy does not prove future forecast performance. Historical count example: observed versus predicted counts with descriptive error metrics. Click to enlarge. Historical count example: annual maps of predicted mean counts. Click to enlarge.

title: 7. Finish the case and keep your evidence
text: Save the checked panel, model settings, software version, map components, workbook, and any derived plots in an output folder. Read Understand results before drafting conclusions, and use R visualization for the plots above. Your next case can be continuous HALE or binary COVID-19 .

title: Choose your starting point
text: New to BSTVC? Read Install & prepare , then follow one case from start to finish. Already have a result workbook? Go to Understand results or R visualization . If an import or model run fails, use the troubleshooting checklist . Each case includes the original data, all required map components, an English companion README, and links back to this guide. Binary and count packages also contain ready-to-import panel CSVs, reshaped without imputation, transformation, or changing measured values. The full conversion procedure remains available for learning and checking. Download all three cases Release notes & checksums ↗

title: What BSTVC helps you examine
text: BSTVC Desktop is a graphical environment for Bayesian analysis of relationships that vary across space and time. It combines local coefficients, global spatiotemporal contribution, and prediction within a common workflow. Standard desktop model fitting does not require R programming; R is optional for customized figures. Research task Question Outputs Local interpretation How do associations vary by location or period? Spatial coefficients (SCs), temporal coefficients (TCs), credible intervals Global contribution Which modeled components contribute to spatiotemporal variation? Spatiotemporal Variance Partitioning Index (STVPI) Dynamic prediction What values does the model estimate for observed or missing outcomes? Predictions, smoothing, imputation, and uncertainty Contribution is not causal attribution. These models describe conditional associations and model-based contributions. They may provide important prior evidence for causal research, but do not establish causal effects on their own.

title: The methodological framework
text: BSTVC stands for Bayesian Spatiotemporally Varying Coefficients . The model represents relationships that can change across locations and periods within one Bayesian hierarchical framework. The source manual calls this a whole-map framework: local estimates are fitted together, with spatial and temporal structure, rather than obtained by fitting an unrelated regression separately to every location. Two ideas guide the analysis. Autocorrelation represents dependence among nearby places or neighboring periods. Nonstationarity allows the relationship between a predictor and the response to differ across those places or periods. Accounting for dependence and estimating variation in relationships answer different questions; a spatially patterned outcome alone does not demonstrate a spatially varying predictor effect. Approach Scope Practical distinction BSTVC Repeated observations across space and time Use a location–time panel and interpret temporal and spatial coefficient outputs. BSVC Spatial observations from one cross-section Use the spatial modeling module for a single time point; repeated years should not be treated as independent map units. STVPI Contribution based on the fitted model Summarize relative spatial, temporal, and combined contributions, with posterior uncertainty. The methods cited in the Chinese manual discuss the STVI, STIVI, STVC, and STIVC model family. These are methodological variants, not interchangeable labels for the three response types in this tutorial. The walkthroughs use the documented desktop controls; consult the method references before selecting or extending a statistical specification. The framework can support interpretation, smoothing, and prediction, including model-based estimates for missing outcomes. Whether it improves prediction or yields useful evidence depends on the data, model assumptions, and validation. Posterior uncertainty describes uncertainty under the fitted model; it does not remove bias from incorrect data alignment, confounding, or an unsuitable neighborhood. For methodological details and programmable extensions, use BSTVC-R . To read the desktop outputs, continue to Understand results .

title: About this guide
text: This English edition consolidates the supplied July 2026 desktop manual with the fuller Chinese online manual, reorganizes their workflows, and checks case filenames, identifiers, dimensions, and missingness against the accompanying data. It targets the English Windows desktop release v2026.8.1. Interface illustrations originate from the supplied manual; historical figures illustrate how to read outputs and are not a new reproduction of model fitting. The spatiotemporal interpretability research organization and BSTVC development team maintains the BSTVC ecosystem. For programmable workflows, see BSTVC-R . Guide revised: 2 October 2026.

title: 1. Install the English desktop release
text: Use Windows 10/11 on an x64 computer. Download BSTVC Desktop English v2026.8.1 from the official GitHub Release. The installer is approximately 548 MB; allow the download to complete before opening it. The examples and online guide are much smaller and can be downloaded separately. Open the downloaded BSTVC_desktop_EN_win_x64_26.08.01_setup.exe . Choose the installation scope offered by the installer. A system-wide installation may require administrator approval. Choose a writable destination folder and select Install . Wait for setup to finish, then select Finish and launch BSTVC using its desktop shortcut. Open Overview to orient yourself before importing data. Prefer a simple folder path and keep enough free disk space for the application, input data, temporary computation, and exported workbooks. Model runtime and memory use depend on data size and model settings; the small count case is a useful first check. English localization of the installation screen in the source manual. The visible 25.1.28 version belongs to that historical illustration; download the current English v2026.8.1 installer linked above.

title: 2. Find your way around the interface
text: The left sidebar selects a module. The main panel on the right displays its upload controls, settings, previews, results, and status messages. Begin with the three-step path at the bottom of Overview: upload data and map, check order, then run models and export. Module Use it for Overview Core features and the recommended workflow Data Input Import panel data, map components, and an optional spatial matrix Data Check Match spatial identifiers and align the panel to map order BSTVC modeling Model panel observations across space and time BSVC modeling Model spatial variation for a single cross-section Data Conversion Reshape repeated time columns from a wide table to a long panel Field Conversion Prepare field names and data types for the model Custom Spatial Matrix Construct or import a neighborhood structure About Software information and project contacts The English desktop overview and module navigation. Click to enlarge.

title: 3. Understand wide tables and panel tables
text: BSTVC modeling expects one row per spatial unit and time point. A wide source table has one row per region, with columns such as COUNT2012 and COUNT2013 . A panel table instead has columns such as GEOID , YEAR , and COUNT , with a separate row for each state and year. GEOID YEAR COUNT 21 2012 180 21 2013 214 37 2012 73 This small illustration explains the structure only; model input order must still be checked against the map. The global HALE download is already a panel. Both original COVID-19 and hepatitis B workbooks are wide tables. Their packages also contain verified panel CSVs for a shorter first run. Wide cross-sectional storage compared with long spatiotemporal panel storage. Click to enlarge.

title: 4. Keep all shapefile components together
text: A shapefile is a collection of companion files, not just a single .shp . For each case, extract the whole ZIP and keep components in the same directory with the same base name. In the map upload control, select all matching components together. Extension Role .shp Spatial geometry .shx Geometry index .dbf Attributes, including spatial identifiers .prj Coordinate reference system .cpg Attribute text encoding .sbn / .sbx Optional spatial index files included with the supplied maps The optional US .shp.xml metadata file is omitted from public packages because it contains local workstation paths. All required map components are retained. Avoid renaming a single companion file, opening only a DBF as your modeling data, or mixing components from different maps. Boundary definitions come from the supplied teaching materials; review geographic scope when using them for your own research.

title: 5. Validate before fitting
text: Use exactly one row for every intended location–time combination. Remove accidental duplicate keys and check missing periods. Ensure the spatial ID exists in both the panel and the map. Match values, field names, and types; preserve leading zeros when present. Keep time in chronological order and select the exact time column you created. Use numeric response and predictor columns. Encode missing values as NA , not zero, an empty label, or a localized text string. For continuous log-Gaussian analyses, check that observed response values are strictly positive. Binary outcomes must be 0/1; count outcomes must be non-negative integers. Inspect missingness and variable definitions. Do not assume that an encoded field name is a raw measurement with the unit suggested by its name. Spatial order is a correctness requirement. A model may finish even when panel rows and map units are mismatched. Successful computation does not prove the mapping is correct. Always run Data Check, then choose Checked Data if the application rearranged observations.

title: 6. Correct field types with Field Conversion
text: A column that looks numeric in a spreadsheet may be imported as text, particularly when numbers are mixed with literal NA , labels, or inconsistent cell formats. Inspect the field properties after input validation. A response or predictor imported as text can cause a later model error with an unhelpful message. Open Field Conversion from the sidebar. Browse to the table that needs correction and select the control to load the field-conversion data. Select one or more response or predictor fields that should contain measurements. Choose numeric as the target type for numeric model variables. Select Start Field Conversion . Compare the original field properties with the converted properties in the result panel. Check the converted values and missing-value counts. Unexpected new NA values indicate cells that could not be interpreted as numbers; correct those source cells rather than silently accepting their loss. Download the corrected table with a new filename. Import it again in Data Input , validate it, and rerun Data Check before fitting. Spatial identifiers have a different role from measurements. Preserve letter codes and meaningful leading zeros, and make their type agree with the map. Do not convert every field to numeric. Field-type conversion also does not rename headers: keep the exact spatial and time field names consistent throughout the workflow.

title: 7. Build and reuse a custom spatial matrix
text: For the polygon examples, default QUEEN-B adjacency is the shortest route. A point map may have no meaningful polygon contacts. Distance-based or k-nearest-neighbor structures can be more appropriate for some study designs, but the choice should reflect the scientific question and geometry. Open Custom Spatial Matrix . Upload the complete map component set and load the map. Inspect the reported number of spatial units, geometry type, coordinate reference system, and geographic extent. Confirm that they describe your intended study area. Choose the supported matrix type and its parameters. The source workflow describes adjacency, fixed-distance, inverse-distance, and k-nearest-neighbor options. For distance settings, check the coordinate system and the distance units indicated by the application; do not assume degrees are metres. Choose the offered weight-standardization setting deliberately. A binary adjacency matrix and a row-standardized matrix encode different weights; record the choice. Select Build Spatial Matrix and inspect the resulting neighbor display. Review isolated locations and connections that do not match the study design. Download the generated .rds matrix. Keep it with the exact map and your construction settings. During input/model configuration, supply that matrix through the custom matrix control. Its rows and columns must correspond to the map units in the same order. Rerun spatial checks after changing the map or matrix. A custom matrix is reusable only with the corresponding unit definitions and order. A matrix built for a different boundary file should not be substituted because its dimensions happen to match. If a k-nearest-neighbor specification fails during INLA computation, review its construction and try a scientifically appropriate alternative in a separately saved run.

title: 8. Understand the nine modeling settings
text: Setting What to choose and record Data Source Choose Raw Data only when the check reports an already aligned order. Choose Checked Data after automatic rearrangement. Response Variable Y Select the outcome you intend to explain or predict, not an identifier or a previously predicted outcome. Explanatory Variables X Select one or more measured predictors with a documented rationale and valid numeric types. Response Type Match the observed outcome: continuous log-Gaussian, binary logistic, or count Poisson for these examples. Time Field Select the actual period column; verify chronology and coverage. Space Field Select the shared spatial ID, with the same name, values, and compatible type in the table and map. Standardize X Variables The demonstrations use Yes. This expresses predictor changes on a standardized scale; preserve the setting when interpreting magnitudes. Spatial Weight Matrix Use default QUEEN-B for the demonstrated polygon cases, or a documented custom matrix matching map order. Threads Start with the demonstrated value of 6 and adjust to available resources; keep the setting in the run record. Standardization makes predictor units more comparable but does not make the predictors causally comparable, remedy confounding, or justify choosing variables only by their resulting rank. Complete the case-specific settings table before selecting Run Model .

title: 9. Choose a sensible thread count
text: The examples use the default QUEEN-B spatial weight matrix: polygon neighbors that touch along an edge or vertex receive a binary adjacency relation. Leave the custom matrix input empty for this route. If the research question calls for distance, inverse-distance, or k-nearest neighbors, use Custom Spatial Matrix and verify that its row/column order matches the map. Start with 6 threads , as shown in the source workflow. More threads can increase overhead and memory demands. Compare similar runs using BSTVC Process Monitor before adjusting. Do not interpret a frozen-looking result panel as proof of failure while the computation is still active. Ready to begin? Choose continuous , binary , or count .

title: The six exported result sections
text: Use Download All Tables after a completed run to preserve the full workbook. Each result section is a worksheet. Exporting only the currently visible table can omit outputs needed for later interpretation. Worksheet What it contains Start by checking model.evaluation Model evaluation and complexity measures Completed model identity, DIC, WAIC, LS, eff/pd2 local.prediction Observed and predicted responses with uncertainty Spatial/time keys, y, predict_y, response scale summary.random.effects Posterior summaries of modeled random effects Component names, means, quantiles time.coefficients Temporal coefficient summaries time_index, explain_variable, posterior quantiles space.coefficients Spatial coefficient summaries Shared map ID and predictor-specific columns STVPI Spatiotemporal contribution estimates Component definitions, percentage scale, uncertainty The source prose sometimes describes coefficients as a wide table, while its temporal plotting code uses a long table with explain_variable . Inspect the exported headers; the companion script checks the illustrated schema and stops if required fields are absent.

title: Model evaluation: compare like with like
text: DIC and WAIC assess model fit with a complexity penalty. Lower values generally support a better comparison within the same response, observations, and likelihood; do not compare the raw values across the three unrelated cases. eff and pd2 are effective-parameter measures used in the source output. Lower complexity alone does not make a model more useful. The manual labels LS as a logarithmic predictive score and describes values closer to zero as favorable under its exported convention. Check the score definition and sign before extending that rule to other software or score implementations. A single score does not replace examining residual structure, uncertainty, missingness, and predictive validation. If model variants use different predictor sets with different missing-value handling, record which observations informed each fit. A visually attractive coefficient map is not a model diagnostic.

title: Coefficients and credible intervals
text: Read the posterior mean alongside the 95% credible interval (2.5th–97.5th posterior quantiles) and the 50% credible interval (25th–75th quantiles). These intervals summarize uncertainty under the fitted Bayesian model; they are not conventional frequentist confidence intervals. Response family Coefficient scale Interpretation caution Continuous log-Gaussian Log response Confirm the transformation and whether a column is a component or a combined coefficient Binary logistic Log odds A coefficient is not a percentage-point change in probability Count Poisson Log modeled mean A coefficient is not directly a change in the number of cases Spatial and temporal components describe different dimensions of variation. Check whether an output field is a random-effect component, a local combined coefficient, or a response-scale prediction before combining or exponentiating it. Standardizing X changes the comparison unit. Keep signs, magnitudes, variable scaling, and posterior uncertainty together in your explanation. For temporal displays, translate time_index to the intended calendar: 1–21 means 2000–2020 for HALE; 1–12 means months of 2020 for COVID-19; 1–12 means 2012–2023 for hepatitis B. A LOESS curve is a visual smoother and adds no posterior certainty. For spatial maps, join on ISO_A3 , gb , or GEOID , according to the case. Do not append coefficient rows to a map by position. Use an intentional legend, show NA areas, and state whether color scales are shared across predictors.

title: Read the contribution component labels
text: Source label How to read it space.X Spatial component associated with predictor X. time.X Temporal component associated with predictor X. space.time.X Combined spatiotemporal contribution associated with predictor X under the exported definition. space.all / time.all Aggregate spatial / temporal components when supplied. space.time.all Aggregate modeled spatiotemporal component when supplied. residual Residual component when included in the fitted response family. Here X is a placeholder for an actual predictor name, such as PD. The source charts show several views of the same modeled decomposition. Do not sum every displayed row as though all rows were mutually exclusive parts: aggregate, combined, and individual components can overlap. Read the export and the method definition together before comparing denominators.

title: STVPI: contribution within the model
text: The Spatiotemporal Variance Partitioning Index decomposes modeled variation into spatial, temporal, and combined components as defined by the model. It supports comparing relative contributions of explanatory factors and reporting their posterior uncertainty. Use the exported component labels and the method reference when describing each part of a chart. The source plotting examples express proportions as percentages. A stored 0.20 is displayed as 20%; do not divide it by 100 again. If your export stores values directly as percentages, adjust the display format rather than guessing from the column name. Preserve the workbook values. A documented limitation for binary and count models. The current source workflow does not include a residual component for logistic and Poisson responses, so the overall model explainable percentage is unavailable for those families. Relative contributions can still be inspected. Do not present them as a complete decomposition of observed outcome variance. Spatiotemporal contribution helps identify patterns that may inform subsequent causal research. It does not establish causal attribution, eliminate confounding, or show what would happen under an intervention. State the outcome, predictor set, neighborhood, missingness handling, and model assumptions when reporting rankings.

title: Prediction columns and response scales
text: Column Meaning in the source workflow y Observed response, including any NA entries predict_y Predicted value or mean on the exported response scale fill_y Outcome field completed with model predictions where observations are missing predict_0.025quant / predict_0.975quant Response-scale 95% interval in the continuous example predict_0.25quant / predict_0.75quant Response-scale 50% interval in the continuous example y_mean and other unprefixed summaries Model-specific summaries; inspect their scale and definition before using them For the continuous case, the manual already back-transforms the predict_ fields. For binary outcomes, predicted probabilities belong on [0, 1]. For counts, inspect whether the prediction is a response-scale mean. Do not apply another log or exponential transformation just to make a plotted value look plausible. Use available observed/predicted pairs for descriptive accuracy. Exclude rows with missing outcomes from such evaluation; an imputed value is not an independent observed truth. For forecasts, future predictor information and a valid hold-out scheme matter. The illustrated desktop workflow alone does not establish a validated forecasting protocol.

title: A practical reporting checklist
text: Software version, response family, response field, and research question. Geographic units, period, sources, map definition, and ID matching. Predictors and their scaling, transformations, missingness, and selection rationale. Neighborhood specification and any differences from the default. Model evaluation, coefficient means, and credible intervals. Available contribution components and the limits on their interpretation. Prediction scale, validation design, metrics, and uncertainty. Saved input, checked data, settings, workbook, and figure-generation script. Continue to R visualization to create the displays, or to Troubleshooting if an output is missing or unexpected.

title: Method references
text: The supplied manual cites the following foundations. Consult the papers for model definitions and assumptions; this practical guide does not replace them. Song, C., Shi, X., & Wang, J. (2020). Spatiotemporally Varying Coefficients (STVC) model: a Bayesian local regression to detect spatial and temporal nonstationarity in variables relationships. Annals of GIS , 26(3), 277–291. Song, C., et al. (2019). Exploring spatiotemporal nonstationary effects of climate factors on hand, foot, and mouth disease using Bayesian STVC model in Sichuan, China. Science of the Total Environment , 648, 550–560. Song, C., et al. (2022). Spatiotemporal disparities in regional public risk perception of COVID-19 using Bayesian STVC series models across Chinese cities. International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction , 77, 103078. Wan, Q., et al. (2022). Spatiotemporal heterogeneity in associations of national population ageing with socioeconomic and environmental factors at the global scale. Journal of Cleaner Production , 373, 133781. Song, C., & Tang, X. (2025). User’s Guide for the BSTVC R Package .

title: Start with the last successful step
text: Identify whether the issue occurred during download, installation, conversion, input validation, order checking, model fitting, export, or plotting. Record the exact message and settings, rather than repeatedly changing several controls at once. Test the compact count case to distinguish an application setup issue from a larger dataset issue.

title: Data or map will not load
text: Symptom Check / action Map missing or empty Extract the ZIP; keep .shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, and .cpg together with one base name; select all required components Source workbook appears to have too many columns It may be a wide table. Use Data Conversion before BSTVC panel modeling Only 31 or 5 records appear These are original wide case rows; after conversion expect 372 or 60 panel records Spatial IDs do not match Compare names, types, whitespace, leading zeros, and every identifier value across panel and map Numeric column contains text Review NA encoding, decimal formats, and spreadsheet cells; use Field Conversion where appropriate Field missing from a selector Check the imported headers exactly, including case and punctuation; confirm Load and Validate Input succeeded Large upload fails The source manual documents a 1 GB upload limit; confirm file size, available memory, and a complete local download

title: Conversion does not match the expected panel
text: Count periods, selected time columns per variable, and resulting rows. The binary case uses 12 columns for each of seven variables; the count case uses 12 for each of five. Select ranges in chronological order, not alphabetical order. Keep invariant IDs separate from time-specific variables. For binary conversion, the original outcome prefix is Covid_binary and the chosen output name is covid . For count conversion, this guide uses YEAR ; if you chose Year , use that exact name throughout. Do not convert an already long ready-panel CSV again.

title: Data Check fails or results look geographically wrong
text: Verify identifier sets, unique location–time pairs, and period coverage. A neighborhood matrix also needs the map’s unit order. If the application rearranged rows, choose Checked Data during fitting. Reusing Raw Data after rearrangement defeats the correction. The continuous map has 177 units with ISO_A3, the China map has 31 units with gb, and the US map has five units with GEOID. A model that finishes with the wrong identifier or row order may still produce invalid-looking scientific conclusions.

title: A model is slow, fails, or returns no table
text: Give a Bayesian local model time to finish; runtime grows with spatial units, time points, predictors, family, and settings. Start with six threads and the default neighborhood. Inspect CPU and memory use if progress is unclear, and preserve any log before restarting. Reduce complexity in a separately saved test, rather than overwriting the research run. Check invalid response values, ID alignment, predictor types, missingness, and available memory. If k-nearest-neighbor settings produce an INLA error or no output, the source manual suggests reviewing the matrix construction or trying a different scientifically appropriate neighborhood. Keep the changed settings in your record. Current BSTVC modeling assumes spatiotemporal nonstationarity for all selected predictors. The source manual describes more selective nonstationarity as future work; do not rely on it as a documented current control.

title: Exported tables or plots are unexpected
text: Export all result tables after the model completes; do not feed a raw case workbook to the visualization script. Check worksheet names and field headers before plotting. Select the time and spatial names from the actual workbook. Check response-scale fields before log/exponential transformations. Binary predictions should be probabilities, not event labels. Use ID joins for geographic plots, and stop on unmatched IDs or duplicate map/spatial keys. Separate the six-predictor continuous tutorial from the manual’s 12-predictor prediction extension. For logistic/Poisson outputs, the overall STVPI explainable percentage is unavailable under the documented residual-component limitation; relative contributions are a different result. Historical illustration metrics will not necessarily match a fresh fit under different software, settings, or missingness treatment.

title: Version boundaries from the Chinese manual
text: The fuller Chinese manual records a 1 GB upload ceiling , the possible k-nearest-neighbor/INLA issue, nonstationarity for all selected BSTVC predictors, and the missing residual component for binary/count models. This guide includes these as documented boundaries, rather than promises about future versions. A 1 GB upload allowance is not a guarantee that a computer can fit a model of that size. For a cross-section, use BSVC modeling; the three detailed tutorials here demonstrate BSTVC panels. The Chinese manual introduces BSVC but does not supply a complete separate BSVC case. Likewise, future selective nonstationarity and an overall binary/count explainable percentage are not taught as available controls. The source installation pictures show an older installer. Use the English desktop release linked in this guide , and report the version you actually run when seeking support.

title: Get useful help
text: For methodological questions or model interpretation, contact Chao Song . For installation, data input, application behavior, or runtime errors, contact Xianteng Tang . Use GitHub Issues for reproducible desktop bug reports. A useful report includes your Windows version, BSTVC version, response family, stage of failure, exact message, dimensions, selected fields, neighborhood, thread count, and a minimal non-sensitive example. Share screenshots with personal paths or private data removed. Do not upload confidential research records just to demonstrate an error. Desktop website · English software release · BSTVC brand, research organization & development team · BSTVC-R

title: 1. Prepare an exported workbook
text: First finish one of the three desktop cases and select Download All Tables. The raw input CSV or wide workbook is not a model result workbook. Install R and use your preferred R editor if you need customized figures. R is optional; use the exported tables directly if you prefer GIS or another analysis environment. Download the English R companion The companion consolidates the source manual’s figure workflows into one script with explicit case settings, portable file selectors, schema checks, ID joins, and response-scale checks. It does not fit models. Its plots will reflect your selected result workbook rather than reproduce the historical illustrations automatically. Run in your own R environment. The supplied data were checked structurally and numerically, and the script syntax was checked. A new full desktop fit and end-to-end execution against freshly exported workbooks are separate steps. If your export uses different headers, inspect it and update the named mapping instead of relabeling columns blindly.

title: 2. Set the case and load the result
text: Install the listed packages once, then open the script. Set case_type to continuous , binary , or count . Run it in your R editor and choose the full result workbook when prompted. It uses worksheet names, not uncertain sheet positions. Near the end, choose the matching map’s .shp file. Copy code # Install once if needed: install.packages(c("readxl", "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "sf", "scales", "pROC")) # In bstvc-visualization.R, choose the case: case_type <- "count" # "continuous", "binary", or "count" # If your manually converted count panel uses Year rather than YEAR, # update settings$time to the exact column name in your result workbook. Time is reconstructed from the source indices: global 2000–2020, binary months 1–12, count 2012–2023. Check that these settings match your actual run. Save images into a separate output folder next to the workbook, and retain the script with your report.

title: 3. Plot coefficients and posterior uncertainty
text: The temporal plot uses time_index , explain_variable , mean , and the four quantile columns. Light shading shows 95% credible intervals; darker shading shows 50%. The optional LOESS display retains the original points. It does not create new posterior estimates. The spatial plot selects exported predictor_mean columns and joins them to the map by the shared spatial key. The script checks that identifiers match, and that map/spatial result keys are unique. Review interval information alongside any mean-only maps. In a GIS workflow, load the map, join the coefficient table using its shared key, verify match counts, and select the intended mean or interval column. Use labels and legends that state the coefficient scale.

title: 4. Plot relative contribution
text: The source STVPI workflow has seven columns: ID, four posterior quantiles, posterior mean, and component name. The companion checks this structure and the proportion scale before creating a contribution plot. Outer and inner interval segments show 95% and 50% credible intervals. If your workbook differs, inspect its original headers and confirm each mapping. Use relative contribution labels for the binary and count workflows. Read the current STVPI boundary before labeling a total explainable percentage.

title: 5. Choose accuracy metrics for the response
text: The script keeps pairs with finite observed and predicted values. These metrics describe the supplied workbook; they do not automatically constitute held-out validation. Response Display / metrics Check first Continuous Observed–predicted scatter, RMSE, R² Use response-scale predict_y, not an already transformed value transformed again Binary ROC and AUC with positive class 1 Both classes are present; probabilities lie between 0 and 1 Count Scatter, MAE, mean Poisson deviance, deviance pseudo-R² Observed counts are integers; predicted means are strictly positive and on the count scale Copy code # Count deviance: handle the y = 0 term explicitly. y <- c(0, 2, 5) mu <- c(0.5, 2.5, 4.5) terms <- mu - y positive <- y > 0 terms[positive] <- y[positive] * log(y[positive] / mu[positive]) - (y[positive] - mu[positive]) mean_poisson_deviance <- mean(2 * terms) mae <- mean(abs(y - mu)) For binary evaluation, the script uses levels = c(0, 1) and direction = "<" for ROC calculation. Higher predicted probabilities therefore correspond to the declared event class. For count pseudo-R², the mean-only reference uses the same evaluated observations; a constant/all-zero response can make that denominator undefined, which is reported as NA.

title: 6. Map predictions with consistent legends
text: Join local.prediction to the map using the spatial key, keeping one result row per location–time combination. Facet by the exact exported time field. Use a common probability range of 0–1 for binary maps. For continuous and count maps, choose a consistent scale that supports comparisons between periods. Display missing values explicitly. Check the joined row count and duplicate keys before plotting. Do not interpret an empty polygon as zero or replace unmatched identifiers with the nearest label. Export figures at a suitable resolution and state the source, model, period, outcome scale, and uncertainty in captions.

title: Complete companion script
text:
You can inspect and copy the full script below. The download above contains the same text. Set your case before running, and confirm exported field names. Show the complete R script Copy code # BSTVC Desktop: optional English visualization companion. # Use exported workbooks, not raw case input tables. No model fitting occurs here. # Install packages once if needed: # install.packages(c("readxl", "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "sf", "scales", "pROC")) # Select continuous, binary, or count; retain the settings matching your own run. case_type <- "count" settings <- switch(case_type, continuous = list(id = "ISO_A3", time = "Year", first = 2000, ntime = 21), binary = list(id = "gb", time = "Month", first = 1, ntime = 12), count = list(id = "GEOID", time = "YEAR", first = 2012, ntime = 12), stop("Choose continuous, binary, or count.")) library(readxl) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(sf) require_fields <- function(data, fields, label) { missing <- setdiff(fields, names(data)) if (length(missing)) stop(label, ": missing fields: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", ")) } cat("Select your exported BSTVC result workbook.
") workbook <- file.choose() sheet_names <- excel_sheets(workbook) expected_sheets <- c("model.evaluation", "local.prediction", "time.coefficients", "space.coefficients", "STVPI") if (!all(expected_sheets %in% sheet_names)) stop("Select a full exported result workbook containing the expected sheets.") read_sheet <- function(name) as.data.frame(read_excel(workbook, sheet = name)) evaluation <- read_sheet("model.evaluation") prediction <- read_sheet("local.prediction") temporal <- read_sheet("time.coefficients") spatial <- read_sheet("space.coefficients") contribution <- read_sheet("STVPI") print(evaluation) str(prediction) output_folder <- file.path(dirname(workbook), paste0("BSTVC-figures-", case_type)) dir.create(output_folder, showWarnings = FALSE) save_plot <- function(p, name, width = 12, height = 8) { print(p) ggsave(file.path(output_folder, name), p, width = width, height = height, dpi = 300, bg = "white") } # 1. Temporal coefficients with posterior credible intervals. require_fields(temporal, c("time_index", "explain_variable", "mean", "0.025quant", "0.975quant", "0.25quant", "0.75quant"), "time.coefficients") if (anyNA(temporal$time_index) || any(!temporal$time_index %in% seq_len(settings$ntime))) stop("Check time_index and the selected case configuration.") temporal$Period <- settings$first + temporal$time_index - 1 temporal$explain_variable <- sub("^time\.", "", temporal$explain_variable) temporal <- arrange(temporal, explain_variable, Period) coefficient_label <- switch(case_type, binary = "Temporal coefficient (log-odds scale)", count = "Temporal coefficient (log-mean scale)", "Temporal coefficient (log-response scale)") p_time <- ggplot(temporal, aes(Period, mean, fill = explain_variable, colour = explain_variable)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .data[["0.025quant"]], ymax = .data[["0.975quant"]]), alpha = .12, colour = NA) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .data[["0.25quant"]], ymax = .data[["0.75quant"]]), alpha = .35, colour = NA) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) + facet_wrap(~explain_variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) + labs(x = settings$time, y = coefficient_label, title = "Temporal associations and posterior uncertainty") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none") save_plot(p_time, "01-temporal-credible-intervals.png") # Optional display smoother. It does not replace posterior means or credible intervals. p_smooth <- ggplot(temporal, aes(Period, mean, colour = explain_variable)) + geom_point(size = 1.5) + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, span = 1) + labs(x = settings$time, y = coefficient_label, colour = "Predictor", title = "Annual estimates with a descriptive smoother") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) save_plot(p_smooth, "02-temporal-display-smoother.png") # 2. Relative spatiotemporal contribution. Column order follows the supplied manual. if (ncol(contribution) != 7) stop("STVPI schema differs from the seven-column source example; inspect names before mapping columns.") names(contribution) <- c("id", "q025", "q25", "mean", "q75", "q975", "effect_name") for (v in c("q025", "q25", "mean", "q75", "q975")) { if (!is.numeric(contribution[[v]])) stop("STVPI quantiles must be numeric; inspect the workbook.") } # Source STVPI exports are proportions. Do not divide these values by 100 again. if (any(contribution$mean < 0 | contribution$mean > 1, na.rm = TRUE)) stop("STVPI scale differs from the source proportion scale; verify before plotting.") p_stvpi <- ggplot(contribution, aes(mean, reorder(effect_name, mean))) + geom_segment(aes(x = q025, xend = q975, yend = effect_name), linewidth = .7, colour = "#b1cfc9") + geom_segment(aes(x = q25, xend = q75, yend = effect_name), linewidth = 2, colour = "#087f79") + geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#15343c") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) + labs(x = "Relative contribution", y = "Modeled component", title = "Spatiotemporal contribution with posterior uncertainty") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) save_plot(p_stvpi, "03-spatiotemporal-contribution.png", height = max(8, nrow(contribution) * .25)) # 3. Prediction accuracy on the exported response scale. require_fields(prediction, c("y", "predict_y", settings$id, settings$time), "local.prediction") if (!is.numeric(prediction$y) || !is.numeric(prediction$predict_y)) stop("Observed and predicted values must be numeric.") observed <- prediction[is.finite(prediction$y) & is.finite(prediction$predict_y), , drop = FALSE] if (!nrow(observed)) stop("No observed/predicted pairs are available for evaluation.") y <- observed$y mu <- observed$predict_y if (case_type == "binary") { if (any(!y %in% c(0, 1)) || any(mu < 0 | mu > 1)) stop("Binary y must be 0/1 and predict_y must contain probabilities.") if (length(unique(y)) != 2) stop("ROC/AUC needs both response classes.") roc_result <- pROC::roc(y, mu, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE) print(pROC::auc(roc_result)) roc_data <- data.frame(FPR = 1 - roc_result$specificities, TPR = roc_result$sensitivities) p_accuracy <- ggplot(roc_data, aes(FPR, TPR)) + geom_path(colour = "#087f79") + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") + coord_equal() + labs(x = "False-positive rate", y = "Sensitivity", title = "ROC curve: positive class = 1") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) } else { if (case_type == "continuous") { sst <- sum((y - mean(y))^2) metrics <- c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((y - mu)^2)), R_squared = if (sst > 0) 1 - sum((y - mu)^2) / sst else NA_real_) } else { if (any(y < 0 | y != floor(y)) || any(mu <= 0)) stop("Count metrics require non-negative integer observations and strictly positive response-scale mean predictions.") deviance_terms <- mu - y positive <- y > 0 deviance_terms[positive] <- y[positive] * log(y[positive] / mu[positive]) - (y[positive] - mu[positive]) mean_deviance <- mean(2 * deviance_terms) null_mu <- mean(y) null_deviance <- if (null_mu > 0) { null_terms <- null_mu - y null_terms[positive] <- y[positive] * log(y[positive] / null_mu) - (y[positive] - null_mu) mean(2 * null_terms) } else 0 metrics <- c(MAE = mean(abs(y - mu)), Mean_Poisson_Deviance = mean_deviance, Deviance_pseudo_R_squared = if (null_deviance > 0) 1 - mean_deviance / null_deviance else NA_real_) } print(metrics) p_accuracy <- ggplot(observed, aes(y, predict_y)) + geom_point(alpha = .55, colour = "#087f79") + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") + labs(x = "Observed response", y = "Predicted response", title = "Observed and predicted values") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) } save_plot(p_accuracy, "04-prediction-accuracy.png") cat("These metrics describe the selected workbook. Independent validation requires a suitable held-out design.
") # 4. Geographic joins must use shared IDs, never row position. cat("Select the matching .shp file. Keep all companion files beside it.
") map <- st_read(file.choose(), quiet = TRUE) require_fields(map, settings$id, "map") require_fields(spatial, settings$id, "space.coefficients") map[[settings$id]] <- as.character(map[[settings$id]]) spatial[[settings$id]] <- as.character(spatial[[settings$id]]) prediction[[settings$id]] <- as.character(prediction[[settings$id]]) if (anyDuplicated(map[[settings$id]]) || anyDuplicated(spatial[[settings$id]])) stop("Map and spatial coefficient identifiers must each be unique.") if (!setequal(map[[settings$id]], spatial[[settings$id]]) || !setequal(map[[settings$id]], prediction[[settings$id]])) stop("Map and result identifiers do not match.") means <- grep("_mean$", names(spatial), value = TRUE) if (!length(means)) stop("No predictor_mean spatial columns found; inspect your output schema.") mapped_coefficients <- left_join(map, spatial, by = settings$id) mapped_coefficients <- pivot_longer(mapped_coefficients, cols = all_of(means), names_to = "Predictor", values_to = "Coefficient") mapped_coefficients$Predictor <- sub("_mean$", "", mapped_coefficients$Predictor) p_space <- ggplot(mapped_coefficients) + geom_sf(aes(fill = Coefficient), colour = "white", linewidth = .1) + facet_wrap(~Predictor, ncol = 3) + scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90") + labs(title = "Spatial associations", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) save_plot(p_space, "05-spatial-coefficient-maps.png", width = 14, height = 10) if (anyDuplicated(prediction[c(settings$id, settings$time)])) stop("Prediction rows must have unique location-time keys.") mapped_prediction <- left_join(map, prediction, by = settings$id) p_prediction <- ggplot(mapped_prediction) + geom_sf(aes(fill = predict_y), colour = "white", linewidth = .1) + facet_wrap(stats::reformulate(settings$time), ncol = 4) + labs(title = "Predicted response across time", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Predicted response") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) if (case_type == "binary") { p_prediction <- p_prediction + scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1), na.value = "grey90") } else { p_prediction <- p_prediction + scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90") } save_plot(p_prediction, "06-predicted-response-maps.png", width = 14, height = 10) cat("Figures saved in: ", output_folder, "
", sep = "")

title: Continue with the evidence
text: Before publishing figures, review the reporting checklist . If the script stops on a missing field, use the export troubleshooting steps ; the check is intended to prevent a plausible-looking plot built from the wrong table.
